signal: Many primality or factorisation queries below a bound, or you need all primes up to about 10^7
why: Cross out multiples of each prime once; every composite is removed by its smallest prime factor, giving near-linear total work.
constraints: n up to about 10^7 in memory and time

signal: Test primality or factorise a single number up to about 10^12
technique: Trial division up to the square root
why: If n has a factor greater than sqrt(n), it also has one smaller than sqrt(n), so checking divisors up to sqrt(n) is enough.

signal: Compute a^b (mod m) where b is huge (up to 10^18)
why: Square the base and consume the exponent bit by bit, so only about log2(b) multiplications are needed.
constraints: use 64-bit or wider intermediates to avoid overflow

signal: Divisibility, simplifying fractions, repeating cycles, or 'smallest common multiple'
why: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) shrinks the numbers geometrically; lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow).

signal: Many queries for C(n, k) modulo a prime larger than n, with n up to about 10^6
why: Precompute n! and its modular inverse once; each C(n, k) is then three multiplications.
constraints: modulus must be prime for Fermat inverses

signal: About n <= 20 items and you must consider every subset (assignment, selection, state of a small set)
why: A subset of n items is an n-bit integer; looping 0 .. 2^n - 1 visits every subset with cheap bit operations.

signal: Subset-sum style question with n around 30 to 40, where 2^n is too slow but 2^(n/2) is fine
why: Split the items in two halves, enumerate each half's 2^(n/2) sums, then combine the two sorted lists with binary search or two pointers.

signal: Generate or count arrangements (permutations, placements, partitions) with constraints, n at most about 12 to 15
why: Extend a partial solution one choice at a time and abandon a branch as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer.
constraints: n up to about 12 to 15 without strong pruning

signal: Every value appears an even number of times except one or two, or you need to toggle and compare states
why: x XOR x = 0 and XOR is commutative, so paired values cancel and only the unpaired survive.

signal: Shortest path in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights
why: Settle the closest unsettled vertex each step; with non-negative weights its distance can never improve later.

signal: Edges or links arrive over time and you must answer 'are these two connected?' or merge groups
why: Path compression and union by size make each operation effectively constant time.

signal: Point updates interleaved with range-sum, range-min or range-max queries
why: A tree over the array answers each query and update by touching only O(log n) nodes.

signal: Choose items with weights and values under a capacity, where greedy by ratio fails and n * capacity is at most about 10^7
why: dp[w] stores the best value achievable with capacity w; process items one at a time, updating capacities from high to low for 0/1 items.

signal: Longest increasing (or non-decreasing) subsequence of an array
technique: LIS with binary search on tails
why: Keep, for every length, the smallest possible tail value; the tails array is sorted, so each element is placed by binary search.

signal: Tasks with 'A must happen before B' dependencies, or a DP over a directed acyclic graph
why: Process vertices in an order where every edge points forward; this also detects cycles when no such order exists.

signal: Find a pattern in a text, or periodicity and borders of a string
why: Reuse the longest border already matched instead of restarting, so the text is scanned once.

signal: Optimise or count something over a rooted tree where a node's answer combines its children's answers
why: A tree has no cycles, so process children first (post-order) and combine their states in the parent.
constraints: n up to 2*10^5; mind recursion depth
